subject: VAL
label: Grade 04
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 04 Values and life skills, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 4 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Honesty and trust
modules.outcome: explain why trust takes time to build
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Honesty and trust', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: explain why trust takes time to build. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Honesty and trust' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: explain why trust takes time to build. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: You break a cup. Honest action: tell the adult straight away, say what happened and offer to help clean. Trust grows when we tell the truth even when it is hard. Method: Model run for 'Honesty and trust'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Explain why trust takes time to build: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Explain what trust is. Trust means believing that a person will be honest and do what they say. Imagine a friend who promises to return your book in 3 days and does. You start to trust that friend a little more.

Step 2, Explain why trust takes time. Trust grows from many small actions, not one big one. If a person keeps 5 promises each week for 4 weeks, that is 20 kept promises. Each one adds a small piece, like laying bricks.

Step 3, Explain how trust breaks quickly. One lie can undo many kept promises, because it makes people wonder what else is untrue. Building a wall takes many bricks; knocking it down can take one push.

Step 4, Explain how to rebuild trust. Admit what happened, say sorry, make it right, and then keep your promises again over time. Example: Hamza breaks a game, tells the truth, and offers to help repair it. Trust returns slowly.

Step 5, Explain with a short example. A student who is always on time, tells the truth about homework and keeps secrets will be trusted with more jobs, like class monitor. Trust is earned by steady behaviour, not by words alone.

Step 6, Your turn: explain in two sentences why a friend who has told 1 lie will need more than 1 day to be trusted again. Answer: one honest day is a small sign; trust grows only when many actions over time show the person can be relied on.

modules.outcome: describe how to help someone who is sad or hurt
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Compassion', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: describe how to help someone who is sad or hurt. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: A classmate drops books. Kind action: help pick them up and say 'Are you OK?'. Reflect: how did it feel for them, and for you? Method: Model run for 'Compassion'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Describe how to help someone who is sad or hurt: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, The scene: At break, Yousef falls and scrapes his knee. He sits on the ground, holds his knee and is crying quietly. Other children walk past because they are busy playing.
Step 2, Notice: Reem stops and looks at Yousef's face. She sees tears and a painful knee. Compassion starts by noticing that someone hurts, and then feeling that you want to help.
Step 3, Choices: Reem could walk on, laugh, call him names, or help. She thinks, 'If I fell, I would want someone to help me.' She picks the choice that cares about his feelings and safety.

Step 4, Help in words and action: She kneels and says gently, 'Are you okay? I will get a teacher.' She stays with him and asks a friend, Omar, to run to the staff room. Words and actions both matter.

Step 5, Result: The teacher arrives in two minutes, cleans the knee and puts on a plaster. Yousef stops crying and says, 'Thank you for staying with me.' Reem did not fix the knee herself, but she got the right help.

Step 6, Sad but not hurt: Another day Yousef is sad because his friend moved away. Reem sits with him and says, 'That sounds hard. I am here.' She listens and does not rush him to cheer up. Compassion includes listening.

Your turn: A classmate drops her lunch and starts to cry. How do you help? Model answer: notice her, say 'That is sad, I am here', ask if she wants help, offer to tell a teacher, and invite her to share your food if allowed.

modules.title: Perseverance
modules.outcome: set a small goal and keep trying
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Perseverance', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: set a small goal and keep trying. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: Empathy steps: notice, ask, listen, say back what you heard, offer help. After a mistake: what happened, what I learned, what I will do next. Method: Model run for 'Perseverance'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Set a small goal and keep trying: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Learn what perseverance means. It means to keep trying even when something is hard or slow. A learner on a bike falls, gets up and tries again. Each try teaches the body something new.

Step 2, Set a small goal. A good goal is clear, small and has a time. Example: 'I will learn 12 spelling words in 4 days.' That means 12 divided by 4, which is 3 new words each day, an easy daily step.
Step 3, Plan the steps. Day 1: words 1 to 3. Day 2: words 4 to 6. Day 3: words 7 to 9. Day 4: words 10 to 12. Write them on a chart and tick each day. Seeing ticks helps you keep going.
Step 4, Meet a problem and keep trying. On day 2 you forget two words. Do not quit. Say, 'I have not learned them yet.' Practise them again, write them 3 times each, and ask a friend to test you.
Step 5, Check the result. After 4 days you test yourself and get 11 of 12 right. That is not perfect, but it is a big step. Celebrate effort, then set the next small goal for the one word you missed.

Step 6, Your turn: set a small goal to read a 24-page story in 4 days and say how many pages per day. Answer: 24 divided by 4 is 6 pages each day; if I miss a day, I read 12 pages the next day and keep going.

modules.outcome: describe how people can be different and equal
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Respecting differences', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: describe how people can be different and equal. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.standard: Describe how people can be different and equal: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Describe how people differ. People can differ in looks, language, food, clothes, family type, age, abilities and interests. Look around the class and name three differences, such as height, favourite sport and the language spoken at home.

Step 2, Describe how people are equal. Equal means everyone deserves fair treatment, respect and the same basic rights, like a safe place to learn. Being different does not make one person worth more or less than another.

Step 3, Learn from a table. Ana speaks two languages, Ben uses a wheelchair, and Chen loves chess. Each has different needs and skills. All three should be allowed to play, learn and speak, so we make space for each one.

Step 4, Notice unfair talk. Calling someone names for how they look or speak is unkind and untrue. A fair response is to say, 'Please stop,' include the person, and tell a trusted adult if it continues.

Step 5, Show respect through actions. Ask a friend to teach you a word in their home language, make a ramp or space for a wheelchair, and offer a game where everyone can join. Count the actions: that is 3 ways to include others.

Step 6, Your turn: describe in one sentence how two classmates can be different and equal. Answer: one may speak Hindi at home and the other English, but both deserve the same respect and the same chance to learn.
